q: In a Linear Programming Problem (LPP), the function to be maximized or minimized is called the:
why: The function being optimized in an LPP is called the objective function.

q: The set of all points satisfying all the constraints of an LPP is called the:
why: The feasible region is the set of points satisfying every constraint simultaneously.

q: In the corner-point method, the optimal value of the objective function occurs at:
o: A corner (vertex) of the feasible region
The centroid of the feasible region
why: For a bounded feasible region, the optimal value always occurs at one of the corner points.

q: Non-negativity constraints in an LPP require that the decision variables satisfy:
why: Decision variables in standard LPP formulation must be non-negative, i.e., x >= 0, y >= 0.

q: If the feasible region of an LPP is unbounded, the maximum of the objective function:
why: In an unbounded feasible region, the objective function may increase without bound, so maximum may not exist.

q: A feasible region is called bounded when it can be:
o: Enclosed within a circle of finite radius
why: A bounded region can be enclosed within some finite circle; otherwise it is unbounded.

q: Which of the following is the correct first step in formulating an LPP?
why: Formulation begins by identifying the decision variables that need to be determined.

q: For a minimization LPP with unbounded feasible region, the minimum value:
o: May exist if feasible region is bounded below in the direction of decrease
why: Even with an unbounded region, a minimum can exist if the objective function is bounded below over the feasible region.

q: The graphical solution method for an LPP with two variables involves plotting:
why: Each constraint is plotted as a line, and the feasible region is the intersection of corresponding half-planes.

q: In an LPP, constraints are typically expressed as:
why: LPP constraints are linear inequalities (or equalities) in the decision variables.
